title: The Critical Period Hypothesis

pts: The Critical Period Hypothesis originally proposed a biologically fixed window, roughly ending at puberty, after which native-like language acquisition becomes impossible.
This was originally proposed primarily for first-language acquisition, based on evidence like recovery patterns after brain injury.
Its extension to second-language acquisition specifically has become the more practically consequential, and more contested, application.
points.who: Eric Lenneberg's original Critical Period Hypothesis

v: Teacher education; trainee teachers or DIET faculty

items: Give groups cards describing key moments: Lenneberg’s proposal, its extension to L2 learning, Johnson and Newport’s study, the census and large-sample studies.
Groups arrange the cards in order and connect them with arrows showing what each added or challenged.
Groups write the hypothesis in its original form and in its L2 form.
Plenary: which version do popular claims usually repeat?

Support: provide the dates on the cards.
Challenge: trainees add one further study they find through Google Scholar.

lines: Original: First-language acquisition depends on brain maturation and becomes very difficult after puberty.
L2 version: Native-like attainment in a second language becomes impossible after a critical age.
T: Which of these was Lenneberg mainly writing about?
S1: The first. The second came later.
T: Yes. The L2 version is the one parents and policy-makers hear.

pts: Age-of-arrival studies generally show earlier L2 learners achieving more native-like ultimate attainment, particularly in pronunciation.
Neurological maturation changes around puberty offer a plausible biological mechanism for such a window.
This evidence is real but doesn't by itself settle whether the effect reflects a sharp critical period or a more gradual decline.

v: A simple sketched graph (not a copy of any published figure)

items: Draw axes on the board: age of arrival (horizontal) and test score (vertical).
Sketch a general pattern: high scores for early arrivals, lower and more varied scores for later ones.
Trainees describe the pattern in two sentences.

Trainees list at least three confounding factors.

Support: provide sentence frames for describing trends.
Challenge: trainees explain why the spread of scores among late arrivals matters.

pts: Some adult learners do achieve remarkably native-like proficiency, challenging the idea of an absolute, impassable cutoff.
Critics argue the age effect may reflect a gradual decline in learning capacity, or confounding social and motivational factors, rather than a sharp biological window.
This connects to Unit 16's young-learners-versus-adults content — the practical differences are real, even if the theoretical explanation remains contested.

points.h: Which Aspects of Language Are Affected
pts: Pronunciation shows the strongest, most consistent age effects; grammar and vocabulary show weaker, more variable ones.
This suggests, if a critical period effect exists, it may not apply uniformly across all dimensions of language.
This nuance matters directly for realistic goal-setting with adult learners across different skill areas.

v: Short recordings of several proficient speakers of English

items: Play four short recordings of proficient speakers from different backgrounds, including Indian speakers.
Learners rate each for ‘accent’ (how different from their expectations) and ‘understanding’ (how easy to follow).
Compare the two sets of ratings.
Discuss: a strong accent does not necessarily mean low intelligibility (Derwing and Munro 2015).
Learners choose one pronunciation feature that affects understanding for them and set a goal.
Learners record themselves and rate their own intelligibility with a partner.
Support: two recordings only, with transcripts.
Challenge: learners identify the features that caused misunderstanding.

lines: Speaker B: strong accent, rated easy to understand. Speaker D: lighter accent, rated harder because of speed.

blocks.x: Pronunciation shows the strongest age effects; grammar and vocabulary show weaker, more variable ones. But intelligibility, which matters most for communication, is achievable at any age (Units 4 and 74).

body: Purpose: to separate accent from intelligibility. Content: two parallel sliders, ‘accent’ and ‘easy to understand’, with four speaker icons placed at different, independent positions on each. Style: clear. Board version: two lines with initials.

body: When Abrahamsson and Hyltenstam (2009) tested late learners who had passed as native speakers to listeners, very few remained indistinguishable once detailed linguistic tests were used. Being taken for a native speaker in daily life and being identical to one on every measure are different achievements, and only the first matters for most learners.

pts: Adult learners can achieve high, genuinely functional proficiency, even if native-like pronunciation specifically becomes statistically less likely with age.
This connects directly to Unit 47's intermediate-plateau work — realistic expectation-setting matters for sustained adult motivation.
Framing this accurately avoids both false discouragement and unrealistic promises about effortless native-like attainment.

v: Goal cards; a simple needs-analysis form

For each, they describe what success looks like.

points.sub: Not a simple 'earlier is always better'
pts: While earlier exposure shows advantages for ultimate pronunciation attainment, this doesn't straightforwardly mean earlier instruction is always optimal for every goal.
Rate of learning and other developmental factors (Unit 16) also matter, independent of ultimate-attainment questions.
Policy decisions about when to introduce foreign-language instruction (Unit 71) should weigh this genuine complexity, not a simplified slogan.

v: Teacher education; DIET faculty or school leaders
Short summaries of two findings; policy statements

items: Present two findings: early starters tend to reach higher eventual attainment with long immersion; in low-exposure classrooms, older starters often progress faster at first (Muñoz 2006).
Distinguish ultimate attainment from rate of learning.

Groups list the conditions (hours, teacher proficiency, materials, home language support) under which an early start would help.

body: When parents ask whether it is ‘too late’ for an older child, answer with both facts: earlier exposure helps pronunciation over many years, and older learners often learn faster in class. Then turn to what can be done now: more reading, more listening, more reasons to use English.

pts: Most current researchers accept some genuine age effect exists while rejecting the strongest, sharpest-cutoff version of the original hypothesis.
This is another area, like Unit 86's UG debate, where confident popular claims often outpace the field's actual, more nuanced consensus.

dek: Unit 87 of 100: is there a biological window after which native-like acquisition becomes impossible? One of SLA's most consequential and genuinely contested questions.

aims.x: This unit examines one of the most consequential questions Universal Grammar raises for teaching: is there a biological window after which native-like acquisition becomes impossible? The answer affects what we promise adult learners, how we set goals, and how policy-makers decide when English should begin in school. The unit separates the evidence from the slogans on both sides.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: state the original Critical Period Hypothesis (CPH) and its extension to second languages;
interpret age-of-arrival evidence and its limits;
distinguish a sharp cut-off from a gradual decline;
explain why pronunciation shows stronger age effects than grammar or vocabulary;
distinguish ultimate attainment from rate of learning;
evaluate claims about early English in school against the evidence;
set honest, motivating goals with adult learners.

why: Why this matters. This question directly shapes expectations for adult learners, and has real, sometimes discouraging implications worth understanding accurately rather than through popular myth.

background.x: Eric Lenneberg (1967) proposed that language acquisition is tied to a period of brain maturation ending around puberty, after which native-like acquisition of a first language becomes very difficult. His evidence came from first-language development and from recovery after brain injury, which is typically better in children than in adults. The hypothesis was about first languages; its extension to second-language learning has proved more consequential for teachers, and more contested.

The best-known L2 study, by Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport (1989), tested Chinese and Korean speakers who had moved to the United States at different ages. Those who arrived in early childhood performed like native speakers on grammaticality judgements; performance declined with later arrival. Later studies complicated the picture. Kenji Hakuta, Ellen Bialystok and Edward Wiley (2003), using large census data, found a steady decline with age of arrival but no sharp break at puberty, and Joshua Hartshorne and colleagues (2018) found a long, gradual decline across a very large online sample. Niclas Abrahamsson and Kenneth Hyltenstam (2009) showed that late learners who pass as native speakers to listeners rarely remain indistinguishable under detailed linguistic testing. Most researchers now accept a real age effect while rejecting the strongest version of the hypothesis (Singleton and Ryan 2004).

A crucial distinction concerns setting. Studies of immigrants measure people immersed in a language for many years. In classroom settings with a few hours of English a week, older beginners often progress faster in the short term than younger ones (Muñoz 2006). Early exposure may favour eventual attainment, especially in pronunciation, but only when exposure is large and sustained.

This matters directly in India. NEP 2020 states that children learn languages very quickly between the ages of two and eight (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020) [VERIFY paragraph 4.12], and many states have introduced English from Class 1. Early multilingual exposure is valuable, but the evidence does not support the belief that an early start in a low-exposure classroom guarantees success, nor that adults who begin later cannot become highly proficient. Many Indian English teachers are themselves evidence of the latter.

items: Evidence summary. A 200-word summary of the CPH for new teachers, distinguishing the original and L2 versions.
Confound analysis. A list of factors, besides age, that could explain an age-of-arrival pattern.
Policy note. A one-paragraph recommendation on the starting age for English, stating conditions.
Goal rewrite. Three adult learners’ goals rewritten to be realistic, specific and measurable.

terms.def: How strongly a listener perceives a speaker’s pronunciation as differing from a reference variety; research shows that a noticeable accent is often fully intelligible, so accentedness and comprehensibility are separate judgements.

The age at which a person first moves into an environment where the second language is widely used; research on the critical period uses it as a key variable when comparing learners’ ultimate attainment.
A factor other than the one being studied that may explain the results; in age research, for example, amount of input may confound the effect of age of arrival.
The hypothesis that there is a limited period in life during which a language can be acquired to native-like levels (Lenneberg 1967); its application to second languages is debated.
The extent to which a speaker’s words can be understood by listeners. Many teachers now aim for international intelligibility rather than a native-speaker accent (Jenkins 2000).

The degree to which a second-language user’s speech or writing is indistinguishable from that of native speakers; it is an unrealistic and unnecessary goal for most learners compared with intelligibility.
How quickly a learner progresses, as distinct from ultimate attainment; older learners often learn faster at first, though younger starters may reach higher levels in the long run.
A period in development when learning a particular aspect of language is easier and more successful, but after which it remains possible. It is a weaker version of the critical period idea.
The final level of proficiency a learner reaches in a second language after long exposure. Research on age often compares ultimate attainment with the rate of learning.
